episode_title: 200 Mark Thompson, CEO Coach and Author: What It Really Takes to Keep the Top Job

real_qa.q: What are the biggest surprises new CEOs face when transitioning to the top job compared to previous executive roles?
real_qa.r: When you get into the big job, you suddenly have 12 bosses on a board of directors instead of one, with much more specific personality dynamics to manage. You don't have visibility on board members even though you may have thought you had intimate relationships with them at board dinners. The biggest surprise is that you have vastly more enterprise-wide stakeholders that you didn't even notice your previous boss was dealing with, requiring a much broader band of understanding and trust-building across diverse stakeholder groups.

real_qa.q: How should newly promoted CEOs build trust with their executive team and board after internal advancement?
real_qa.r: The key is recognizing that peers who thought they might get the job need significant relationship investment and recontraction. You must earn followership and partnership by understanding that each stakeholder group—shareholders, HR, brand, operations—tests you on three dimensions: can they trust you, are you competent, and do you feel comfortable telling them the truth. This requires moving beyond defending your own budget and instead genuinely engaging with the different lenses and concerns each role brings to the table.
real_qa.requete: CEO build trust executive team board

real_qa.q: What did Mark Thompson learn about the definition of success from his national and global research study with Wharton?
real_qa.r: Thompson and his research team discovered that success is not actually money, fame, and power, as commonly believed, but rather a combination of three elements: purpose larger than yourself (serving customers or a community), passion (something you secretly love doing), and performance (the competitive drive to win). These three grounding elements create the unlock moments that drive sustained achievement, not financial or status rewards.
real_qa.requete: Mark Thompson success definition Wharton study

real_qa.q: How did Mark Thompson's learning disability become a superpower in his entrepreneurial career?
real_qa.r: Thompson had an eyesight issue that placed him in special classes and made traditional education difficult, making him feel irrelevant. His unlock moment came when he realized that learning disabilities could be superpowers—discovering this through working with disabled entrepreneurs like Charles Schwab, who created online stock trading to make investing simpler and more accessible. This realization shaped his earlier entrepreneurial career to find other disabled entrepreneurs who could change the world because they saw problems through a simpler lens.
real_qa.requete: Mark Thompson learning disability superpower entrepreneurship

real_qa.q: What role did Silicon Valley's entrepreneurial culture play in shaping Mark Thompson's early leadership philosophy?
real_qa.r: Growing up in Silicon Valley when it was still fruit orchards, Thompson was influenced by an entrepreneurial setting rooted in the gold rush mentality and later the space program's existential mission to put a man on the moon. This created a culture of risk-taking, invention, and innovation where people in garages (like Hewlett Packard in Palo Alto) were solving existential crises. This fertile valley of technology and innovation deeply shaped his belief that great leaders share curiosity and the conviction that there is always a better way to do things.
real_qa.requete: Silicon Valley entrepreneurship space program influence
